opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference comes down to what you can observe and how expensive it is to observe it. With knowledge work, the inputs and outputs are mostly digital. A model reads documents, writes a memo, produces some code, and you can capture that whole process, run it thousands of times, and compare the results against what an expert would have done. You can build a benchmark fairly cheaply, and if the model fails, nothing really breaks. You just run it again.

Construction is different because the world pushes back. A task like framing a wall isn't one clean output. It depends on the materials that showed up that day, the weather, the condition of the site, and the people working around you. You can't easily reset the environment and try again a thousand times, and mistakes can be costly or dangerous. Simulation helps, but there's always a gap between the simulator and a real job site, so a good score in simulation doesn't tell you as much as you'd like. A lot of the quality is also hidden or delayed. You may not know whether something was done well until an inspector checks it, or until a problem shows up years later.

That said, I wouldn't overstate how easy knowledge work is to evaluate. Passing a test is not the same as doing a job. Real professional work is often ambiguous, with no single right answer, and it plays out over long stretches with lots of context and collaboration. A polished report can still be wrong in subtle ways, and it can take a real expert a long time to notice. So in both domains, the question that matters is the same: did the work actually achieve its goal under real-world conditions? The principle carries over, but the measurement looks very different.

For knowledge work, I think we should move toward realistic, multi-step tasks judged by domain experts, and eventually toward real economic outcomes. For physical work, we need to evaluate the whole system, meaning perception, planning, and manipulation together, and we need to include safety and reliability from the start. There, a 95% success rate might sound impressive, but if the remaining 5% includes a dangerous failure, that system isn't ready to be deployed.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts digital knowledge work with construction’s changing physical conditions, but does not characterize the task spaces as discrete versus continuous.

r002.rationale: It says digital work can be captured and benchmarked cheaply, but does not explain that language, math, or code proficiency makes those environments easier to simulate.

r003.rationale: It describes physical complexity and simulation gaps in construction, but does not attribute easier knowledge-work simulation to avoiding real-world physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big difference comes down to where the hard part lives. With knowledge work, the thing you're evaluating is almost entirely in the digital world. The input is text or code or a spreadsheet, the output is text or code or a spreadsheet, and so the model can actually do the whole task end to end inside a computer. That's why benchmarks like SWE-bench were possible to build. You take a real GitHub issue, you let the agent make changes in a repo, you run the unit tests, and you get a fairly objective signal about whether it worked. The environment is the evaluation.

Physical tasks are different in a couple of ways. First, you can't just scale them. If I want to run a thousand evaluations of a coding agent, I spin up a thousand containers. If I want to evaluate whether a system can frame a wall or run plumbing, somebody has to actually be in a building, and the cost of a mistake is a flooded basement, not a failed test. So you end up relying on simulation, and the gap between simulation and the real world is still a big open problem. Things like friction, deformable materials, the fact that a two-by-four is never perfectly straight, those are hard to model and they're exactly the things that break you.

The second difference is that in knowledge work, the model is the whole system. In construction, the AI is one component sitting on top of hardware, sensors, actuators, and the failure modes get entangled. If a robot drops a brick, was that perception, planning, or a motor issue? That makes attribution really hard when you're trying to understand what the intelligence actually contributed.

And then there's a subtler point about what the task even is. For a lot of knowledge work, we have a decent sense of what "done" looks like, even if the grading is fuzzy. A legal memo, a pull request, a research summary. For a physical task, success is often spread across time and context. The wall has to be plumb today, but it also has to not crack in five years. So the evaluation horizon is much longer and much harder to compress into a benchmark.

What I find interesting, though, is that the agent framing that came out of language models is starting to carry over. The question in both cases is really the same: can the system take actions, observe consequences, and correct itself? We just happen to have a much faster feedback loop in software right now, which is a big part of why progress there looks so much faster.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts digital knowledge work with physical construction, but does not describe their task spaces as discrete versus continuous.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge tasks can run inside a computer, but does not attribute easier simulation to models’ proficiency in English, mathematics, or code.

r003.rationale: It explains that physical simulations struggle with friction, deformable materials, and other real-world details, while software tasks can be evaluated digitally with benchmarks and tests.

astra-6.text:
I think a key difference is how clearly we can define and measure success. In construction, you have a physical outcome: did you build the structure correctly, does it meet the specifications, is it safe? Those things aren’t always easy to verify, but there are concrete constraints you can test against.

With knowledge work, the output can be much harder to judge. If an AI writes a report, being fluent or sounding convincing doesn’t necessarily mean it did a good job. You have to ask whether the facts are correct, whether it addressed the right question, and whether it actually helped someone make a decision. And there may be several equally good answers.

At the same time, physical tasks introduce challenges that a text-based evaluation can miss: uncertainty in sensing, changes in the environment, and actions that are costly to undo. So I’d distinguish the difficulty of doing a task from the difficulty of evaluating it. A physical task can be extremely hard to perform while having a relatively clear success criterion; a knowledge task can produce an impressive-looking answer whose value is much harder to establish.

r001.rationale: The response compares how success is evaluated, but does not contrast continuous physical tasks with discrete language-based tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss models’ proficiency in English, mathematics, or code, or how that proficiency makes tasks easier to simulate.

r003.rationale: It mentions physical-world uncertainty and costly actions, but does not explain simulation difficulty in terms of real-world physics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is how you measure success. With a physical task like construction, there are concrete constraints: does the structure stand, does it meet the specifications, and can you build it safely? That doesn’t make evaluation easy, but there’s a physical reality that grounds it.

With knowledge work, the goal can be much less precise. If an AI writes a report, what makes that report good? Is it factual accuracy, clarity, originality, or whether it helps somebody make a decision? Those things can depend on the person and the context. And producing something that looks convincing isn’t necessarily the same as doing the job well.

So I’d want to evaluate the whole task: can the system use the available information, recognize what it doesn’t know, and produce an outcome that’s useful? In both settings, you need to test beyond a narrow benchmark. But in knowledge work, defining the outcome you actually care about is often a substantial part of the challenge.

r001.rationale: It contrasts concrete physical constraints with less precise knowledge-work goals, but does not describe either task space as continuous or discrete.

r002.rationale: It does not mention language, math, or coding proficiency making knowledge-work environments easier to simulate.

r003.rationale: It notes that physical tasks are grounded in reality, but does not attribute easier simulation of knowledge work to avoiding real-world physics.
